\[
f(x)=2\prod_{i=1}^n (x-r_i),

\[

\]

so

\[
r_1r_2\cdots r_n=\pm 33.
\]

Thus the roots are distinct integers whose product has absolute value \(33=3\cdot 11\). The possible relevant roots are among \(\pm1,\pm3,\pm11\), with at most one of each.

Also,

\[
a_{n-1}=-2(r_1+\cdots+r_n),
\]

so we want the least possible absolute sum of the roots.

To get product \(\pm33\), we must use one of \(\pm3\) and one of \(\pm11\), possibly with some of \(1,-1\). The best cancellation occurs with roots

\[
3,\,-11,\,1.
\]

Their product is

\[
3(-11)(1)=-33,
\]

which is valid, and their sum is

\[
3-11+1=-7.
\]

So

\[
|a_{n-1}|=2|{-7}|=14.
\]

No smaller absolute sum is possible because the two non-\(\pm1\) roots must sum to at least \(8\) in absolute value, and the \(\pm1\) terms can reduce that by at most \(1\).

\[
f(x)=2\prod_{i=1}^n (x-r_i).
\]

The constant term gives

\[
2(-1)^n r_1r_2\cdots r_n=66,
\]

so

\[
(-r_1)(-r_2)\cdots(-r_n)=33.
\]

Let \(s_i=-r_i\). Then the \(s_i\) are distinct nonzero integers with product \(33\), and

\[
a_{n-1}=2\sum_{i=1}^n s_i.
\]

So we need minimize \(\left|\sum s_i\right|\).

The absolute values of the \(s_i\) must multiply to \(33=3\cdot 11\), so the relevant possibilities are:

- include \(\pm 33\), giving large sum;
- include \(\pm 3\) and \(\pm 11\), possibly with \(\pm 1\)’s.

If \(3\) and \(11\) have the same sign, the sum is at least \(14-1=13\) in absolute value.  
If they have opposite signs, their sum has absolute value \(8\), and adding a \(\pm 1\) can reduce it to \(7\).

This is achieved by

\[
s_i=-3,\ 11,\ -1,
\]

since

\[
(-3)(11)(-1)=33,\qquad -3+11-1=7.
\]

Then

\[
|a_{n-1}|=2|7|=14.
\]
